narrative:
The model estimated a 49.0% chance that you will leave, which is borderline but high enough to be treated as a flight-risk signal in the promotion decision. This is not a certainty; it means your profile currently looks close to someone who may move on rather than someone firmly staying.

The strongest influence on the prediction was your total years of experience. Your 1–5 years is common among employees predicted to stay—about half have that level—so this factor actually pushed toward staying. The next most important factor was whether you have other job opportunities. You reported having them, while only about 23% of employees predicted to stay did, so this was the main top-three factor pushing toward leaving. Third was whether you felt you received the promotion you deserved. You said yes, and this matched a majority of stayers, so it also pushed toward staying. Even so, the outside-opportunity signal and other retention-risk aspects of your profile were enough for the model to classify you as likely to leave.

The organization should not treat a 49% estimate as proof you will quit. Before denying promotion, it should discuss your career path, the outside opportunities you are seeing, and the low satisfaction, stability, and reward signals in your profile. You should ask for a clear promotion timeline and retention plan.
